PRIVILEGED AND CONFIDENTIAL — ATTORNEY WORK PRODUCT

REDLINE REVIEW MEMORANDUM

To: Funds & Asset Management Practice — Deal Team
From: [Firm] Transactional Counsel
Date: [Current Date]
Re: Counterparty Markup of Investment Advisory Agreement — Redline Review
Matter: Funds Asset Management — MATTER FILE 15

I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY

This memorandum provides a comprehensive redline review of the counterparty's markup of the investment advisory agreement against our firm's standard form and internal playbook. The counterparty's revision accepts most firm-standard provisions but introduces three substantive deviations that require careful analysis: (i) a reduction in the indemnification cap and conversion of the basket from a deductible to a tipping basket; (ii) expanded carve-outs to the Material Adverse Effect (MAE) definition targeting regulatory action; and (iii) a shortened survival period for core representations. 

Pursuant to the controlling deal-team instruction (the latest message in the correspondence thread), our client will concede the basket conversion but treats any survival-period reduction as a walk-away issue. The schedules and exhibits qualified into the base materials control over general statements and must be reconciled against each deviation.

This memorandum is organized as follows: Section II outlines the scope and materials reviewed. Section III analyzes each deviation in detail with recommendations. Section IV sets forth the recommended negotiation strategy informed by the internal playbook and partner directives. Section V provides a summary of positions.

II. SCOPE AND MATERIALS REVIEWED

We have reviewed the following materials in connection with this matter:

• Base Materials — the firm-standard form investment advisory agreement and internal playbook of record for funds asset management matters.

• Counterparty Markup — the counterparty's redline against the standard form, which accepts most firm-standard provisions while introducing three identified deviations.

• Schedules and Exhibits — the disclosure schedules qualifying the base materials, including Schedule 3.7 (pending regulatory inquiries), Schedule 5.2 (retained liabilities), and Exhibit B (survival matrix). Per the matter materials, scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials.

• Deal Team Correspondence — the partner email thread. The latest message controls and provides: (1) the client will concede the basket conversion; and (2) any survival-period reduction is a walk-away issue.

• Unrelated administrative correspondence was misfiled into this matter folder and expressly must NOT be relied upon for this analysis.

III. DEVIATION ANALYSIS

A. DEVIATION 1 — INDENIFICATION CAP REDUCTION AND BASKET CONVERSION

1. Description of the Markup

The counterparty's revision introduces two changes to the indemnification provisions: (a) the aggregate indemnification cap is silently reduced from the firm-standard amount; and (b) the basket is converted from a true deductible to a tipping basket.

2. Analysis Against Standard Form and Playbook

Under the firm-standard form and internal playbook, the indemnification cap is set at the negotiated aggregate amount, and the basket operates as a true deductible: losses must exceed the basket threshold before any indemnification becomes payable, and once the threshold is exceeded, the indemnifying party is only responsible for amounts in excess of the threshold. The counterparty's conversion to a tipping basket would materially alter the risk allocation: under a tipping basket, once losses aggregate past the threshold, the indemnifying party becomes liable for the entire amount (including amounts below the basket threshold). While this may appear to benefit the indemnified party, it must be evaluated in light of the simultaneous cap reduction.

Schedule 5.2 lists retained liabilities that the markup's indemnification changes would silently shift. The interaction between the reduced cap and the basket conversion must be carefully analyzed against these scheduled retained liabilities. If the retained liabilities are material and the cap is reduced, the client could face unrecoverable losses above the reduced cap even where the indemnification obligation would otherwise apply. The basket conversion, while seemingly favorable, does not offset this concern because it primarily affects recoverability of losses below the basket threshold, not losses above the cap.

3. Deal Team Instruction

Per the controlling instruction from the deal-team correspondence, the client will concede the basket conversion (i.e., accept the change from a deductible to a tipping basket). This position supersedes any earlier communication indicating the opposite ordering.

4. Recommendation

■ Basket Conversion: ACCEPT. The client has instructed that the basket conversion may be conceded. The tipping basket, in isolation, marginally benefits the indemnified party (our client). We should therefore not resist this change.

■ Cap Reduction: REJECT. The silent reduction in the indemnification cap is not supported by any deal-team instruction and directly undermines the protections available under Schedule 5.2's retained liabilities. We should counter with the firm-standard cap as set forth in the base materials. If the counterparty insists on a reduction, this should be escalated for partner review, given the interaction with Schedule 5.2 liabilities.

5. Risk Assessment

The combination of (a) reduced cap and (b) basket conversion creates a one-sided risk profile in which the counterparty obtains meaningful downside protection through the cap reduction while nominally conceding on the basket structure. The client's position conceding the basket removes one potential negotiating lever, making the cap reduction the critical battleground on this deviation.

B. DEVIATION 2 — MATERIAL ADVERSE EFFECT CARVE-OUTS FOR REGULATORY ACTION

1. Description of the Markup

The counterparty's revision adds carve-outs to the definition of Material Adverse Effect for regulatory action "of exactly the kind at issue in this matter." This is a targeted modification intended to remove from the MAE definition certain regulatory events that would otherwise qualify as MAEs.

2. Analysis Against Standard Form and Playbook

The firm-standard MAE definition contains standard exclusions that are appropriate for the funds asset management context (e.g., general market conditions, changes in applicable law, acts of war or terrorism). The counterparty proposes adding carve-outs for regulatory action of the kind at issue — i.e., regulatory inquiries or investigations that could otherwise constitute MAEs.

Schedule 3.7 discloses two pending regulatory inquiries that intersect precisely with these proposed carve-outs. The scheduled disclosures are material to this analysis because: (a) the client has already disclosed these pending regulatory inquiries; (b) the counterparty is aware of them; and (c) the proposed MAE carve-outs would effectively neutralize the client's ability to rely on adverse regulatory developments as an MAE, which is particularly problematic where those inquiries are already pending and could escalate.

The scheduled exceptions, which control over general statements in the base materials, underscore the significance of the regulatory exposure. If the MAE carve-outs are accepted, the client loses a meaningful remedy if the pending regulatory inquiries escalate into material adverse outcomes during the applicable period.

3. Deal Team Instruction

There is no express deal-team instruction on the MAE carve-outs.

4. Recommendation

■ REJECT, or in the alternative, NARROW. The proposed MAE carve-outs are too broad in that they target "any" regulatory action rather than only regulatory actions arising from general changes in law or regulation applicable to the industry. We should:

(a) REJECT the blanket carve-out for regulatory action of the kind at issue;

(b) If the counterparty insists on some regulatory carve-out, counter with a version that: (i) excludes only regulatory actions not attributable to the counterparty's own conduct or which were pending and disclosed prior to signing; and (ii) preserves the client's right to assert an MAE based on regulatory action that materially and adversely affects the client's business.

(c) Ensure that Schedule 3.7 disclosures are preserved in the final documentation and that the carve-outs do not absolve the counterparty with respect to the disclosed regulatory inquiries.

5. Risk Assessment

This deviation is highly material. Accepting the proposed MAE carve-outs without limitation would expose the client to the risk that pending regulatory inquiries escalate into material adverse consequences without triggering any MAE-based remedy. This is particularly acute given that the Schedule 3.7 inquiries are already pending and their potential outcomes are unknown.

C. DEVIATION 3 — SURVIVAL PERIOD REDUCTION FOR CORE REPRESENTATIONS

1. Description of the Markup

The counterparty's revision introduces a new, shortened limitation period that reduces the survival window for the core representations from the firm-standard period established in Exhibit B of the schedules and exhibits.

2. Analysis Against Standard Form and Playbook

Exhibit B sets the survival matrix for the agreement, establishing the applicable survival periods for core versus non-core representations. The firm-standard form and playbook establish specific survival periods designed to protect the client's ability to pursue claims for breach of representation following closing.

The counterparty's limitation-period change contradicts Exhibit B's survival matrix. Under standard market practice and the internal playbook, reductions to survival periods for core representations are disfavored because core representations address fundamental aspects of the transaction (e.g., authority, title, capitalization) and are typically subject to longer survival periods.

3. Deal Team Instruction

Per the controlling instruction from the deal-team correspondence: any survival-period reduction is a WALK-AWAY issue. The client treats the ability to maintain the full survival period for core representations as a non-negotiable term. This is the most critical deviation in the markup.

4. Recommendation

■ REJECT — WALK-AWAY. Any reduction to the survival period for core representations under Exhibit B is a walk-away issue per the controlling deal-team instruction. We must:

(a) Reject the counterparty's limitation-period change outright;

(b) Reaffirm that the survival matrix in Exhibit B controls, as scheduled exceptions control over general statements in the base materials;

(c) Be prepared to walk away from the transaction if the counterparty does not withdraw or modify this change.

5. Risk Assessment

This is the highest-priority deviation. The survival periods under Exhibit B are fundamental to the risk allocation negotiated in the base materials. Accepting a shortened survival period for core representations would significantly impair the client's ability to bring claims for breaches that might only surface after the shortened period expires. The deal team's characterization of this as a walk-away issue confirms its critical importance.

IV. NEGOTIATION STRATEGY

Based on the analysis above and the controlling deal-team instructions, we recommend the following negotiation strategy:

1. Priority 1 — Survival Period (Walk-Away Issue). Firmly reject the counterparty's limitation-period change. Reaffirm that Exhibit B's survival matrix controls. Take the position that this term is non-negotiable and that the client would rather walk away than concede on the survival periods for core representations.

2. Priority 2 — Indemnification Cap. Reject the silent cap reduction. Counter with the firm-standard cap from the base materials. If the counterparty pushes back, point to Schedule 5.2 retained liabilities as evidence that the cap reduction would result in a material under-allocation of risk. Escalate to partner review if a compromise is necessary.

3. Priority 3 — Basket Conversion (Client Concession). Concede the basket conversion from deductible to tipping basket as instructed. This should be deployed as a good-faith concession to facilitate progress on more important items.

4. Priority 4 — MAE Carve-Outs. Reject the blanket regulatory-action carve-outs as drafted. Counter with a narrower version that: (a) does not cover regulatory actions arising from the counterparty's own conduct; (b) expressly excludes the Schedule 3.7 pending inquiries from any carve-out; and (c) preserves the client's ability to assert an MAE based on material adverse regulatory outcomes.

V. POSITION SUMMARY

Deviation | Counterparty Proposal | Client Position | Recommendation
----------|---------------------|-----------------|----------------
Indemnification Cap | Silent reduction | Reject — preserve standard cap | Counter at firm-standard cap
Basket Conversion | Deductible → Tipping | Concede | Accept as instructed
MAE Carve-Outs | Add regulatory carve-outs | Reject / narrow | Counter with limited carve-out
Survival Period | Shortened for core reps | Walk-away | Reject — non-negotiable

VI. OPEN ITEMS AND NEXT STEPS

1. Confirm the specific dollar amounts for the firm-standard cap and counterparty's reduced cap for quantification in any escalation memorandum.

2. Obtain the specific text of the counterparty's proposed MAE carve-out language for precise counter-drafting.

3. Confirm with the deal team whether there are any additional instructions regarding the MAE carve-out negotiation.

4. Prepare counter-redline reflecting the positions set forth in Section V above.

Respectfully submitted,

[Firm] Transactional Counsel
Funds & Asset Management Practice

This memorandum is privileged and confidential, prepared in anticipation of litigation and for the purpose of legal advice. Do not distribute outside the legal team without approval.
